segments.text: [serious] Which country gets the most tourists in the world? France. And yes, that’s the right answer. But who’s second? The United States? No. Italy, with Rome and Venice? Not that either. China? Wrong again. Second place belongs to a country with 49 million residents that welcomes almost twice that many visitors every year: 97 million. Spain. And those tourists bring in €135 billion a year. More than Russia makes exporting natural gas. But Spain is much more than beaches. Five hundred years ago, it built history’s first empire on which the sun never set, stretching from Mexico to the Philippines, from the Netherlands to Argentina. Today, Spanish has more native speakers than any language except Chinese. Half a billion people speak it. Spain gave the world a man who dresses half the planet and ranks among the ten richest people on Earth.

[serious] It has the world’s second-largest high-speed rail network, behind China. The highest life expectancy in the European Union. And the most decorated soccer club in history. But is everything really that sunny? In 2013, one in four Spaniards was unemployed. Among young people, it was one in two. Spain has one of Europe’s lowest birth rates. Entire provinces in the interior are emptying out. Every few years, some part of the country wants to break away. Young people can’t rent apartments in their hometowns because those apartments are being rented to tourists instead. And in the fall of 2026, that very issue brought down the government. So how did a country that lost the world’s greatest empire learn to live better than many of the countries that defeated it? And what’s the price? Let’s start with the map.

[serious] The Iberian Peninsula is roughly square, cut off from the rest of Europe by mountains. To the north, the Pyrenees form a barrier stretching about 270 miles. For centuries, there were barely any proper roads through them. That helps explain why Spain has always been something of a world unto itself. The French have an old saying: “Africa begins at the Pyrenees.” On the other three sides, there’s water: the Atlantic, the Mediterranean, and a strait just nine miles wide separating Spain from Africa. Now look at an elevation map. Spain has the second-highest average elevation in Europe, after Switzerland: about 2,200 feet above sea level. Why? Because the entire middle of the country is the Meseta, a vast plateau sitting roughly 2,000 to 2,600 feet up. Dry, with hot summers and cold winters.

[serious] There’s a saying about it: nine months of winter and three months of hell. Madrid sits right in the middle of that plateau. And that’s no accident. In 1561, King Philip II moves the capital to an otherwise unremarkable town in the geographic center of the country. The most popular explanation? To keep it equally distant from everyone, so no province could claim to be more important than the others. Washington and Canberra would follow the same basic logic, centuries later. And here’s the first thing to understand about Spain. For centuries, it’s had more rock than water. Its rivers—the Tagus, the Ebro, the Guadalquivir—run low in summer. Much of the country is semidesert, good for olives, grapes, and grazing sheep. Which helps explain why Spain is now the world’s largest olive oil producer, responsible for almost half the global supply.

[serious] It has more land planted with vineyards than any other country. And it’s Europe’s largest pork producer. Think jamón, Spain’s famous dry-cured ham. Black pigs grazing in oak groves and eating acorns do much better in the dry south than cattle do. So where do the people live? Around the edges, of course. Along the coasts and in the valleys. Consider this: 85 percent of Spaniards live on 30 percent of the land. Greater Madrid has 7 million people. Greater Barcelona, 5 million. Then there’s Valencia, Seville, Bilbao. But inland, on the Meseta, entire provinces have population densities comparable to Siberia. They call it “Empty Spain.” Villages with ten retirees left. Shuttered schools. One bus a week.

[serious] Over the past 50 years, the interior has lost half its population. The government has even created a ministry tasked with doing something about it. Everyone moved to the coast, where the tourists—and the jobs—are. Now for the history. Because without it, none of this makes sense. The year is 711. Arab and Berber forces cross that narrow strait from Africa. Within a few years, they conquer almost the entire peninsula. For the next eight centuries, southern Spain is part of the Islamic world. In the 10th century, Córdoba is Europe’s largest city, with half a million residents, libraries, and paved streets with streetlights. Meanwhile, in Paris, pigs are wandering through the mud. Arabic numerals, algebra, oranges, rice, and cotton reach Europe through here.

[serious] Spanish still has 4,000 words of Arabic origin. Think of the Alhambra in Granada. Or even, according to one theory, “olé,” derived from “Allah.” The Christian kingdoms in the north spend 800 years slowly taking the land back. The Reconquista. It ends in 1492, with the fall of Granada. And two more things happen that same year. In the spring, Queen Isabella expels all Jews who refuse to convert to Christianity. In the summer, she gives three ships to a persistent Genoese sailor named Columbus. And Spain hits the jackpot. It becomes the first to discover America. Half a century later, a mountain of silver is discovered at Potosí, in what is now Bolivia. Silver starts pouring into Europe on a scale the world has never seen. The Spanish silver peso becomes the first global currency, accepted in China, India, and the Ottoman Empire.

[serious] Even the dollar sign, “$,” is borrowed from the Spanish peso. The empire spreads across four continents. It looks like it will last forever. So what happens next? Spain develops a condition that, 400 years later, will be called Dutch disease. Here’s how it works. A huge flood of money enters the country. Money extracted from the ground, rather than earned by making things. So why bother making anything? Wool goes to the Netherlands to be woven. Spain buys back the finished cloth. Weapons come from Italy. Foreigners build the ships, too. Silver flows through Spain like water through a pipe, ending up with bankers in Genoa and Antwerp. At home, all that money drives prices up fivefold in a century. The nobility considers work beneath them. Better to be a penniless nobleman than a wealthy merchant. And guess who else gets expelled?

[serious] In 1609, the Moriscos, descendants of Muslims: 300,000 of the south’s most skilled farmers and craftspeople. In the name of religious purity, Spain throws out people who actually know how to make things. Add endless wars across Europe in defense of Catholicism. The supposedly invincible Spanish Armada, defeated by the English and battered by storms in 1588. Four government bankruptcies in a single century. And the empire that looked eternal starts to deflate. In 1898, the United States takes Cuba, the Philippines, and Puerto Rico from Spain in just three months. In Spain, they have one word for it: “the Disaster.” An entire generation of writers and philosophers wrestles with the same question: How did we go from being the world’s leading power to being nobody? The 20th century starts even worse.

[serious] A poor, largely agricultural country splits into two camps. Republicans, anarchists, and Communists on one side. The Church, the military, landowners, and monarchists on the other. In 1936, that division erupts into civil war. Three years. Half a million dead. Guernica, bombed by German aircraft before World War II even begins. The military wins, led by General Francisco Franco. He will rule for 36 years, until his death in 1975. Under Franco, Spain lives two completely different lives. For the first twenty years, he builds a closed economy designed to produce everything at home. The result? Hunger, rationing, and a GDP lower than before the war. The rest of Europe gets the Marshall Plan and a postwar boom. Spain becomes a pariah, barred even from joining the United Nations until 1955. Then, in 1959, everything changes.

[serious] A group of technocrats from the Catholic organization Opus Dei persuades the aging dictator to open the economy. Restrictions come down. Foreign companies are invited in. And most importantly, the beaches open for business. A sunny, cheap, safe country, just a two-hour flight from rainy London and Hamburg. “Spain is different,” the slogan says. And the Germans and the British arrive by the millions. The 1960s become known as the Spanish Miracle. Annual growth hits 7 percent. Only Japan is growing faster. Farmworkers from Andalusia head for construction jobs at coastal hotels and factory jobs in Barcelona. Benidorm, once a fishing village, becomes a forest of high-rises. SEAT starts building cars under license from Fiat. Suddenly, every family has a car.

[serious] In fifteen years, Spain transforms from an agricultural country into an industrial one. And here’s a detail that tells you more about Spanish life than almost any statistic. Why do people eat dinner at 10 p.m.? Why does the summer sun set at 10:30? Franco. In 1940, as a gesture of solidarity with Hitler, he moves the clocks to Berlin time. Geographically, Madrid is west of London. It should be on Greenwich time. More than eighty years later, nobody has moved the clocks back. So the entire country lives an hour out of sync with the sun. People get up in the dark, eat lunch at three, and have dinner at ten. And that famous siesta? Mostly a myth. Only one in six Spaniards takes an afternoon nap. With a schedule like that, a midday break is just how you make it to dinner. Franco dies in his bed in 1975.

[serious] And this is where Spain pulls off something very few countries have managed. King Juan Carlos, the man Franco personally chose as his successor, helps turn Spain into a democracy in just three years. All political parties are legalized, including the Communists. A new constitution is written. They call it “the Transition.” It’s still studied as a model for leaving a dictatorship behind with very little bloodshed. In 1981, armed military officers storm parliament and try to turn back the clock. The king goes on live television in uniform and says no. The coup collapses overnight. Then comes Spain’s fast track into Europe. In 1986, it joins the European Community, and European funding pours in. Hundreds of billions for roads, bridges, airports, and trains.

[serious] In 1992, Barcelona hosts the Olympics. Seville hosts the World’s Fair. And Spain launches its first AVE high-speed train, from Madrid to Seville. Since then, the high-speed network has grown to about 2,500 miles, the second-largest in the world. Madrid to Barcelona, roughly 375 miles, takes two and a half hours. All right, you might say. But what actually pays the bills in Spain today? It’s the eurozone’s fourth-largest economy, behind Germany, France, and Italy, at around $1.7 trillion. And for the past three years, it’s been growing faster than any other major European Union economy, while Germany has been standing still. First, tourism. Obviously. It accounts for roughly 12 to 13 percent of the economy, a bigger share than the auto industry contributes in Germany.

[serious] The Balearic Islands have a million residents and receive 16 million visitors a year. Sixteen tourists for every local. Every year. Second, fashion. Meet Amancio Ortega. The son of a railroad worker, he drops out of school at thirteen to become a tailor’s apprentice. In 1975, he opens his first store in A Coruña. Today, his company, Inditex, owns Zara, Bershka, Massimo Dutti, and Pull&Bear. More than 5,500 stores in a hundred countries. Ortega himself moves between first and second place among Europe’s richest people, depending on how shares in his French rival Bernard Arnault’s company are doing. What was his big idea? Fast fashion. A new collection reaches stores in two weeks, instead of the usual six months. See it on the runway, and fourteen days later, it’s hanging in the mall.

[serious] Half the production stays close by, in Spain, Portugal, and Morocco, to keep things moving. Everyone else will eventually copy that model. And Ortega isn’t an isolated case. Spain knows how to take an ordinary mass-market product and build a global business around it. The supermarket chain Mercadona, barely known outside the country, controls a quarter of Spain’s grocery market. It regularly ranks among the world’s most efficient retailers. Talgo makes trains that run in Saudi Arabia, Kazakhstan, and the United States. Telefónica owns Brazil’s largest telecom operator. And Spanish construction companies—the same ones that helped inflate the bubble back home—went abroad after the crash. Now they build subway lines in London, highways in Texas, and airports in Australia.

[serious] The crisis drove them out of Spain and turned them into global players. Third, banking. Santander and BBVA are among Europe’s biggest banks. But most of their profits come from Latin America, from countries like Mexico and Brazil. It’s a kind of conquest in reverse. Five centuries ago, the Spanish came for silver. Now they come for interest payments. Fourth, energy. That dry, sunny Meseta turns out to be perfect for solar panels. The coast is ideal for wind turbines. Today, more than half of Spain’s electricity comes from renewable sources, one of the highest shares among major countries. At midday, when the sun is shining, wholesale electricity prices regularly fall to zero. Then again, in the spring of 2025, the entire country, along with Portugal, lost power for several hours. A total blackout.

[serious] Trains, subways, traffic lights, airports—everything stopped. And people are still arguing about whether the country moved away from conventional power plants too quickly. Fifth, Spain is Europe’s vegetable garden. Look at the southeast from space. That white patch near Almería isn’t snow. It isn’t salt. It’s greenhouses. About 74,000 acres covered in plastic. The largest concentration of greenhouses on Earth, visible from orbit. Here, in Europe’s driest corner, with less rainfall than some deserts, farmers grow tomatoes, cucumbers, and peppers all winter for Germany, Britain, and Scandinavia. Add oranges from Valencia, strawberries from Huelva, and peaches from Catalonia. Spain is the European Union’s largest exporter of fruits and vegetables. And the world’s largest producer of olive oil. With one catch.

[serious] In 2023, drought wipes out half the harvest, and olive oil prices double. A roughly one-quart bottle costs €10 at the store. For a Spaniard, that’s like the price of bread doubling. Water is the single biggest constraint on Spain’s economy. In 2024, Barcelona declares a drought emergency. Catalonia’s reservoirs fall to 15 percent of capacity. So Spain builds Europe’s largest desalination plants and transfers water between rivers over hundreds of miles. The same old problem: more rock than water. Only now, it’s hotter, too. And then there are cars. Spain is Europe’s second-largest automaker, behind Germany. There’s SEAT, now owned by Volkswagen, plus factories run by Renault, Ford, and Stellantis. More than 2 million vehicles a year. Now let’s talk about the price of all this.

[serious] And we have to start in 2008, because you can’t understand Spain’s problems without it. In the 2000s, Spain goes through an unprecedented construction boom. Cheap loans in euros. Tourists. Immigrants. Everyone is building, everywhere. In 2006, construction starts on 800,000 homes. More than in Germany, France, and Britain combined. Construction provides one in eight jobs. In Ciudad Real, a city of 75,000 people, they build a billion-euro international airport. It operates for three years, then closes. The passengers never materialize. Spain has several of these ghost airports. Entire neighborhoods of new housing where nobody has ever lived. And when the bubble bursts in 2008, Spain falls harder than any European country except Greece. Unemployment hits 26 percent. Youth unemployment reaches 55 percent.

[serious] More than half of people under 25 are out of work. Half a million families are evicted over unpaid debts. Hundreds of thousands of young, educated Spaniards move to Germany and Britain to work as waiters. An entire generation gets labeled “ni-ni”—neither in school nor working. Spain borrows €40 billion from Europe to rescue its banks. It takes ten years to climb out. Today, unemployment is around 11 percent, still the highest in the European Union. Why? Tourism and construction mean seasonal, low-paying work. A hotel opens in May and hires you. It closes in October and lets you go. Until recently, one in four employment contracts was temporary, a European record. A 2022 reform brought that down, but the habit stuck.

[serious] So a thirty-year-old Spaniard with an engineering degree often still lives with their parents, with neither a permanent job nor a mortgage. The average age for moving out in Spain is thirty. In Sweden, it’s twenty-one. Which brings us to the second problem: housing. This is where everything comes full circle. Those 97 million tourists need somewhere to sleep. So apartments in central Barcelona, Málaga, and Palma are being turned into short-term vacation rentals en masse. For an owner, renting to a tourist for €1,000 a week beats renting to a student for €800 a month. In major cities, rents have risen by 50 to 100 percent in ten years. Wages have risen by 10 percent. In the summer of 2024, Barcelona residents take to the streets and spray tourists with water guns. Their signs say: “Tourists, go home.”

[serious] The city promises to eliminate all 10,000 licensed tourist apartments by 2028. In the Canary Islands and the Balearics, there’s serious discussion of visitor caps and taxes on every hotel night. By the fall of 2026, housing has become a national political crisis. Protesters set up a tent camp in Madrid’s main square. Parliament rejects the government’s housing decrees. Prime Minister Sánchez calls an early election. The problem is that one in eight workers depends on tourism. Cutting it back threatens their livelihoods. Letting it keep growing means pushing residents out. The third problem is children. Or, more precisely, the lack of them. Spain’s fertility rate is 1.1 children per woman, one of the lowest in the world. Lower than Japan’s. The average age for having a first child is thirty-two, the highest in Europe.

[serious] And it makes sense. If you’re still living with your mom at thirty and working on a temporary contract, when are you supposed to start a family? Immigration is the only thing keeping the population from shrinking. Half a million people arrive every year, mostly from Latin America: Venezuela, Colombia, Peru. They speak the same language, share a Catholic background, and tend to integrate quickly. Others come from Morocco and elsewhere in Africa, across the sea. Today, almost one in five people living in Spain was born abroad. And compared with many other Europeans, Spaniards have been relatively relaxed about it. So far. The fourth problem is a country that keeps threatening to come apart. Spain has seventeen autonomous regions. Each has its own parliament. Some have their own language, police force, and tax system.

[serious] Catalonia. The Basque Country. Galicia. The 1978 constitution gives them almost everything except the right to leave. For forty years, the separatist group ETA terrorizes the Basque Country, killing 850 people, before finally announcing its dissolution in 2018. Then there’s Catalonia. In 2017, it holds an independence referendum that Madrid declares illegal. Police beat voters outside polling stations. Catalonia’s parliament declares a republic. Within hours, its leaders flee to Belgium. Those who stay are imprisoned, then pardoned, then granted amnesty—to secure their side’s votes in parliament. That’s Spanish politics for you. One of the country’s richest regions, producing a fifth of its GDP, doesn’t want to subsidize the poorer south. And every ten years or so, it makes sure everyone remembers.

[serious] But that’s only part of the political picture. For forty years after Franco, two parties alternate in power: the Socialists and the conservative People’s Party. A familiar setup if you live in Britain or the United States. Then comes the 2008 crisis. Millions lose their jobs. Young people fill the squares. New parties emerge from the protests, and the two-party system breaks apart. The result? Four elections between 2015 and 2019, because nobody can put together a government. Pedro Sánchez, prime minister since 2018, held on through a coalition of half a dozen parties, including Catalan and Basque nationalists. Every vote came with a price. An amnesty. A tax concession. More regional powers. The country hadn’t managed to pass a new budget since 2023. Meanwhile, on the other end of the spectrum, Vox was gaining ground.

[serious] It wants to abolish regional autonomy, close the borders, and restore a “united Spain.” One side pulls the country apart. The other wants to force it back together. In October 2026, the whole arrangement collapses. Sánchez calls an election for November 29. Polls suggest that, for the first time since democracy returned, a far-right party could enter the government. And yet, through all of this, the economy keeps growing faster than Germany’s. Apparently, it doesn’t much care who’s in charge in Madrid. The fifth problem is memory. Franco died fifty years ago, and Spaniards still haven’t agreed on what to make of him. Until 2019, he lay in an enormous mausoleum carved into a mountainside by political prisoners, beneath a cross nearly 500 feet tall. His remains were removed.

[serious] Across the country, people are still searching for and opening unmarked graves from the Civil War. There are more than 2,000. The left wants a reckoning with the past. The right says to leave it alone. And a party nostalgic for that era is the third-largest in parliament. It may soon be in government. Now for geopolitics. Here, Spain is surprisingly quiet. It belongs to NATO and the European Union, but generally prefers trade to war. It has two cities in Africa, Ceuta and Melilla, the last European possessions on the continent. Every year, thousands of migrants try to force their way across the border. Then there are the Canary Islands, off the African coast. Tens of thousands of people from Senegal and Mali cross the Atlantic in wooden boats to reach them. In 2024, almost 50,000 arrived, a record.

[serious] It’s one of the deadliest migration routes in the world. Human rights groups estimate that thousands never make it. Spain is Europe’s southern door. And Brussels pays Morocco to help keep that door mostly closed. Spain also has a never-ending dispute with Britain over Gibraltar, taken in 1713 and never returned. And it has a special relationship with Latin America: twenty countries that speak its language. That’s Spain’s greatest source of soft power. Half a billion people for whom Madrid feels, in some small way, like home. Plus soccer. Real Madrid is the most decorated club in history, with fifteen European Cups. And when Real plays Barcelona, people watch in two hundred countries. So what’s the secret? How does a country that lost everything end up living better than so many others?

[serious] Let’s look at the numbers where Spain really does come out on top. Life expectancy: eighty-four years, the highest in the European Union. By 2040, it’s projected to rank first in the world. Why? Mediterranean food. Olive oil. Sunshine. Free healthcare considered among the best on the planet. Spain has led the world in organ donation for thirty years running. It’s one of Europe’s safest countries. And one of its most accepting. Spain legalized same-sex marriage in 2005, the third country in the world to do so. A Catholic country that spent decades under a dictator ruling in the name of the Church. So the Spanish seem to have made an unusual choice. They didn’t become a great power again. Their economy isn’t the most efficient. Their jobs aren’t the most secure. Their politicians fight. Their regions want to leave.

[serious] But they live longer than everyone else. They eat exceptionally well. They have dinner at ten and go out at midnight with the whole family, kids included. There’s a saying: Spaniards live to enjoy life. Germans live to work. An oversimplification, obviously. But when German retirees move to the Spanish coast in droves to spend their remaining years, and Spaniards don’t do the reverse, you start to see who actually won that argument. Five centuries ago, Spain conquered half the world and got little out of it beyond inflation and war. Today, it conquers no one. And half the world comes to Spain voluntarily. Pays, sunbathes, and goes home. Maybe that’s what a real empire looks like. A place the world comes to because it wants to.
